To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we identified and characterized two new trimeric autotranporters from E. coli, EhaG and UPAG, and we found that these two proteins are expressed at high levels in different E. coli strains and are important for the virulence of these bacteria.

the EhaG TAA, a positional orthologue from enterohemorragic E. coli O157:H7, is a novel adhesin that promotes adherence to epithelial cells, biofilm formation and aggregation and that it is a member of a family of adhesins with diverse functions.

the trimeric autotranporter proteins EhaG and UPA-G from pathogenic Escherichio coli have been characterized and that the proteins display differential cellular binding, sequence divergence in their passenger domains, and expression that is significantly enhanced in an H-NS mutant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular characterization of the Eha and Upa G trimeric autotranporters from the enterohaemorrhagic and the uropathogenic strains of Escherichia Coli respectively.
the characterization of the Eha and Upa G trimeric autotranporter proteins from the pathogenic Escherichiacoli.
the characterization of the EhaT and UpaT trimeric autotansporter proteins from pathogenic Escherichio coli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the EhaG protein has a different function than the UpaG protein, and that the two are not orthologues.
EhaG and UPA G are two TAAs with similar properties and function, but with different binding specificities, and with different expression profiles.

UpaG and its homologues from UPEC strains are more likely involved in the colonization of the urinary tract while the Eha and its homologs from EHEC strains may be more important for the colonization of the gut.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have identified and characterized the first two members of a new family of trimeric autotranporter adhesins that are important for the pathogenicity of uropathogenic and enterohemorrhageic Escherichia col.
EhaG and its homologues are likely important in EHEC pathogenesis, while UpaG and its homlogues may have a role in UPEC pathogenesis.

we have shown that the EhaG/UpaG TAA family is a large family of proteins that is found in all E. coli pathovars and that these proteins can be divided into subfamilies based upon their sequence divergence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TAAs represent a diverse family of proteins with a wide range of functions that are adapted to the different niches of E. coli pathogenesis.
the EhaG TAA is a novel cell surface adhesin that may contribute to the virulence of EHEC.

the EhaG TAA from EHEC and the UpaG TTA from UPEC are important virulence determinants of their respective pathotypes and that they represent promising targets for the development of novel anti-virulence strategies.
